title: Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:1–16)
hookLine: jealousy, a field, a killing, and the question: am I my brother's keeper?

cards: The first family outside the garden has two sons. Cain, the older, works the ground, like his father. Abel, the younger, keeps sheep.

One day both bring an offering to God: Cain some of the fruit of the ground, Abel the firstborn of his flock, and the fat portions. And God, the story says, has respect for Abel and his offering, but not for Cain and his.
Cain's face falls. He's furious, with the heat of watching a brother get the praise you wanted. This story is about that heat, and what it does in a field.

teach.h: WHY ABEL'S? THE TEXT IS QUIET.
teach.b: Why was Abel's offering accepted and Cain's not? Genesis doesn't say. Readers have guessed: Abel gave the firstborn, the best; Cain's heart was wrong.
The letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith. But the text itself is quiet.
What it does record is God speaking to Cain before anything happens, in the King James Bible: "If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door."
Sin, crouching at the door like an animal, and God adds: you must rule over it. Cain still has a choice. Then Cain talks with his brother in the field, and kills him.
And God comes with a question again, the way he did in the garden: "Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?" Keeper.
In Hebrew, shomer, from shamar, the same root as the garden: to keep, to guard. Adam was put in the garden to keep it. Cain refuses to keep his brother.
And God answers: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground." Abel never speaks in the story. Not one word.
Even his name, Hevel, is the Hebrew word for breath, or vapor. But his blood speaks.
Then the surprise: Cain is sent away to wander, and he's afraid someone will kill him, so God puts a mark on him.
Not a brand of shame. A protection. Even the killer isn't left without care.
Christian preachers have answered Cain's question for him, and today's line takes their answer: yes, you are.

how: Christians often hear the story of Cain and Abel as a call to responsibility for one another, and preachers turn to it when speaking about violence, jealousy and care for neighbors in need.

games.q: you're Cain. your face has fallen, you're furious, and God says sin is crouching at the door. what's still true?
o: it's too late; it's already decided.
you can still rule over it.
games.why: "if thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted?" God speaks to Cain before anything happens. the choice is still his.

practice: Think of a sibling, or someone who's been like one, a cousin, an old roommate, a friend from way back, and notice what you feel: warmth, distance, an old jealousy, an argument never finished.
Don't fix it now; just hold them in mind, and find one real question you'd want to ask them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

carryVoice: Your line: you are your brother's keeper. By blood or by choice, a brother counts. That's day three hundred forty-one.
